newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-PUMPED-UP CHANG BURSTS FLAT-BALL THEORY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PUMPED-UP CHANG BURSTS FLAT-BALL THEORY.

text.p: The top men's players at the Australian Open spent most of the first week worrying about flat balls and the slow-paced court. But not Michael Chang.

A pumped-up, lightning-quick Chang, who is seeded second, powered his way into the fourth round to keep on track for a final against top seed Pete Sampras and revenge for his last grand slam disappointment.
The devout right-hander is on a mission.

Chang went a short way to avenging his loss to Sampras in last year's U.S. Open final when he beat his fellow American in a warm-up event last week, but victory in the Australian Open would be much sweeter.
The stocky baseliner has failed to convert three grand slam finals into titles since winning the 1989 French Open as a 17-year-old, but he feels the time is right.
With defending champion Boris Becker, a shock first round loser, out of the bottom half of the draw, Chang has a much smoother ride towards the final.
Becker, who crashed to Spaniard Carlos Moya in a five-set thriller on the first day of the tournament, started the ball-bashing campaign.
He was followed by a stream of other top players including Sampras, who also criticised the Rebound Ace hardcourt surface for being too slow.
Tournament organisers said that as far as they could tell the balls and the courts were the same as last year.
And Chang was baffled by the fuss.
"For the most part I'm pretty pleased with everything -- balls, nets, courts. Stick me on a tennis court, I'm happy," said the world number two.
In the most hyped match of the tournament, Chang ruthlessly destroyed Britain's great new hope Tim Henman in straight sets, simply running down everything his opponent could produce.

His next tie, against Ukrainian hitman Andrei Medvedev, could be the toughest he will face before the final. The towering Medvedev has been having the time of his life in Melbourne, knocking out 15th seed Michael Stich of Germany in the second round.
In the top half of the draw, Sampras enjoyed an easy first round match, but struggled early against Romania's Adrian Voinea before winning in four sets.
However, in the third round the 25-year-old was at his awesome best, losing only two games to world number 28 Mark Woodforde of Australia, a semifinalist here last year.

Sampras faces a much more difficult passage to the final than Chang, with double Open champion Jim Courier, world number three Goran Ivanisevic, Austria's Thomas Muster and Wayne Ferreira of South Africa all still alive in his half of the draw.
A Spanish Armada sailed into Melbourne at the start of the week and three of their 15 players remain in the men's draw -- giant-killer Moya, 10th seed Albert Costa and 14th seed Felix Mantilla.
